source.title: Open Problems in Geometry of Curves and Surfaces

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a closed C^2 surface in Euclidean 3-space R3 that is flexible, meaning that it admits a continuous deformation through C^2 surfaces that preserves its intrinsic metric, where "closed" means compact and without boundary?

evidence.quote: To state the problem explicitly, let us say that a surface is (isometrically) flexible, within a given smoothness class, if it admits a continuous deformation which preserves its smoothness and does not change its intrinsic metric.

No one, however, has ever found a flexible closed surface in the smoothness class C2, or even C1,1, where by closed we mean compact without boundary. Hence the following question: Problem 1.1 (Euler [54], 1776; and Maxwell [124], 1819). Does there exist a closed C2 surface in Euclidean space R3 which is flexible?

accepted.question_text: Are all smooth tight surfaces in Euclidean 3-space R3 rigid, where the source describes tight surfaces as smooth surfaces with total positive curvature 2π that are natural higher-genus analogues of convex surfaces?

evidence.quote: This method was used by Alexandrov [7] to establish the rigidity of analytic surfaces with total positive curvature 2π (e.g., tori of revolution) which are also known as tight surfaces [33, 113, 29], and are natural higher genus analogues of convex surfaces.
Problem 1.2 (Alexandrov [7] 1938; and Nirenberg [140] 1962). Are all smooth tight surfaces in R3 rigid?

accepted.question_text: Are negatively curved annuli in R3 that are bounded by a fixed pair of convex planar curves necessarily rigid under isometric deformation?

evidence.quote: Problem 1.3. Are negatively curved annuli bounded by a pair of fixed convex planar curves rigid?

accepted.question_text: Let Γ be a smooth closed curve immersed in R3 with a continuous one-to-one binormal vector field B. Must the ribbon determined by Γ and B be twisted, in the sense that the linking number of Γ with the offset curve Γ + εB is nonzero?

evidence.quote: Suppose that we have a smooth closed curve Γ immersed in R3 which admits a continuous family of osculating planes, i.e., planes which contain the first and second derivatives of Γ. Then the binormal vector field of Γ may be defined as any continuous vector field which is orthogonal to these osculating planes.

Problem 1.4. Let Γ be a smooth closed curve immersed in R3. Suppose that Γ has a continuous binormal vector field B which is one-to-one. Does it follow then that the ribbon (Γ, B) is twisted? In other words, must the linking number between Γ and Γ + εB be nonzero?

accepted.question_text: Given a positively curved Riemannian metric on the disk, what condition must a space curve satisfy in order to be the boundary of an isometric embedding of that disk into Euclidean 3-space?
accepted.context_brief: Prescribed boundary for positive curvature disk

evidence.quote: Problem 1.5 (Yau [189], 1990). Given a metric of positive curvature on the disk what is the condition on a space curve to form the boundary of an isometric embedding of the disk?

accepted.question_text: Does every space curve in R3 that bounds a surface of positive curvature have at least four points at which the torsion vanishes?
accepted.context_brief: Zero torsion points on boundary curves

evidence.quote: Problem 1.6 (Rosenberg [157], 1993). Does every curve bounding a surface of positive curvature in 3-space have (at least) four points where the torsion vanishes?

accepted.question_text: Do there exist nonconvex surfaces that remain rigid after finitely many points are deleted, and in particular are punctured analytic tight surfaces such as a torus of revolution rigid?

evidence.quote: Problem 1.7. Are there some nonconvex surfaces which remain rigid after finitely many points of them have been deleted. For instance, are punctured analytic tight surfaces, such as a torus of revolution, rigid?

accepted.question_text: Can every smooth 2-dimensional Riemannian manifold be isometrically embedded in Euclidean 4-space R4?

evidence.quote: Problem 1.8 (The global isometric embedding problem, Yau [189] 1993; Gromov [82]). Can every C∞ 2-dimensional Riemannian manifold be isometrically embedded in R4?

accepted.question_text: Given a smooth metric in a neighborhood of a point of a 2-dimensional Riemannian manifold, does some neighborhood of that point admit an isometric embedding into Euclidean 3-space R3?

evidence.quote: Problem 1.9 (The local isometric embedding problem). Given a C∞ metric in a neighborhood of a point in a 2-dimensional Riemannian manifold, does there exist an isometric embedding of some neighborhood of that point into R3?

accepted.question_text: For which subsets A of the sphere Sn does there exist an immersion f: M -> R^(n+1) of a closed oriented n-manifold whose Gauss map G_f has image contained in A, so that G_f(M) is an A-directed spherical image?

evidence.quote: To every (C1) immersion f : Mn → Rn+1 of a closed oriented n-manifold M, there corresponds a unit normal vector field or Gauss map Gf : M → Sn, which generates a set Gf(M) ⊂ Sn known as the spherical image of f. Conversely, one may ask:
Problem 2.1 (Gromov [82]). For which sets A ⊂ Sn is there an immersion f : M → Rn+1 such that Gf(M) ⊂ A? Such a mapping would be called an A-directed immersion of M [53, 81, 158, 177].

accepted.question_text: Let f: M -> R^(n+1) be a closed oriented hypersurface with Gauss map G_f, and for each unit vector u define the shadow S_u = { p in M | <G_f(p), u> > 0 }. If every such shadow is connected, must the image f(M) be convex?

evidence.quote: Then for every unit vector u ∈ Sn (corresponding to the direction of light) the shadow (or shade as it is known in computer vision [98]) is defined as (1) Su := { p ∈ M | <Gf(p), u> > 0 }.
Problem 2.2 (Wente [187], 1978). Does connectedness of the shadows imply that f(M) is convex?

accepted.question_text: Let M and M' be smooth orientable closed surfaces in R3. If there is a diffeomorphism f: M -> M' that preserves both Gauss curvature and the Gauss map, does it follow that M and M' are congruent?

evidence.quote: Problem 2.3. Let M, M0 ⊂ R3 be smooth orientable closed surfaces. Suppose there exists a diffeomorphism f : M → M0 which preserved the Gauss curvature and the Gauss map. Does it follow then that M and M0 are congruent?

accepted.question_text: Let P and P' be polyhedral surfaces in R3. If corresponding faces of P and P' are parallel and have the same area, does it follow that P and P' are congruent?

evidence.quote: Problem 2.4. Let P, P0 ⊂ R3 be polyhedral surfaces. Suppose that the faces of P and P0 are parallel and have the same area. Does it follow then that P and P0 are congruent?

accepted.question_text: Is every convex polytope unfoldable, meaning that one can cut its surface along some spanning tree of edges and isometrically flatten the result into the plane without overlaps?

evidence.quote: If P admits such a one-to-one unfolding (for some choice of T) then we say that P is unfoldable.
Problem 3.1 (Dürer [49], 1525; Shephard [170], 1975). Is every convex polytope unfoldable?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a reasonably simple intrinsic algorithm for detecting which geodesics between pairs of vertices of a convex polyhedron are realized as its edges?
accepted.context_brief: Intrinsic edge detection for convex polyhedra

evidence.quote: Dürer’s problem is that it is essentially an intrinsic question, yet there is no known intrinsic method to detect the edges of a convex polyhedron.
Problem 3.2. Does there exist a reasonably simple algorithm for detecting the edges of a convex polyhedron intrinsically?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a convex polyhedron that has a pseudo edge graph which cannot be unfolded without overlap?

evidence.quote: Problem 3.3. Does there exist a convex polyhedron with a pseudo edge graph which is not unfoldable.

accepted.question_text: Among all convex surfaces with a fixed intrinsic diameter, is the surface of greatest area a doubled disk?
accepted.context_brief: Area maximizer at fixed intrinsic diameter

evidence.quote: Problem 4.1 (A. D. Alexandrov [8]). Of all convex surfaces with a fixed intrinsic diameter, is the one with the greatest area a doubled disk?

accepted.question_text: Let S be a closed surface in R3 of constant width and fixed area. How small can the volume of S be?
accepted.context_brief: Minimum volume at fixed area and constant width

evidence.quote: Problem 4.2 (Volume of surfaces of constant width). Let S ⊂ R3 be a closed surface of constant width and fixed area. How small can the volume of S be?

accepted.question_text: Let S be a closed surface in R3 with diameter d. Suppose there exists a constant h < d such that whenever two parallel planes at distance h both meet S, the area of the portion of S lying between those planes is constant. Must S be a sphere?

evidence.quote: Problem 4.3 (Surfaces with strips of constant area). Let S ⊂ R3 be a closed surface of diameter d. Suppose that there exists a constant h < d so that whenever a pair of planes separated by a distance of h intersect S, the area of S contained between these planes is constant. Does it then follow that S is a sphere?

accepted.question_text: For a space curve γ in R3, let its width w be the infimum of the distances between pairs of parallel planes that bound γ, and let its inradius r be the supremum of the radii of spheres contained in the convex hull of γ and disjoint from γ. What is the shortest possible curve with a prescribed width or a prescribed inradius?
accepted.context_brief: Shortest space curve with given width or inradius

evidence.quote: These are well-known open problems ... in classical geometry of space curves γ : [a, b] → R3, which are concerned with minimizing the length L of γ subject to constraints on its width w and inradius r respectively. Here w is the infimum of the distances between all pairs of parallel planes which bound γ, while r is the supremum of the radii of all spheres which are contained in the convex hull of γ and are disjoint from γ.
Problem 5.1 (Zalgaller [192] 1994). What is the shortest curve in R3 with a given width or inradius?

accepted.question_text: If Γ is a closed curve of fixed length L in R3, how large can the volume of the convex hull of Γ be?
accepted.context_brief: Maximum convex-hull volume of closed curve

evidence.quote: Problem 5.2 (Volume of the convex hull of closed curves). Let Γ be a closed curve of fixed length L in R3. How big can the volume of the convex hull of Γ be.

accepted.question_text: Let Γ be a closed curve of fixed length L in R3, and let A be the area of the convex hull of Γ. Is A maximized exactly when Γ is a circle, with the convex hull interpreted as a doubly covered disk?
accepted.context_brief: Maximum convex-hull area of closed curve

evidence.quote: Problem 5.3 (Area of the convex hull of closed curves). Let Γ be a closed curve of fixed length L in R3, and A be the area of the convex hull of Γ. Show that A is biggest when Γ is a circle, in which case we consider the convex hull of Γ as a doubly covered disk.

accepted.question_text: Is every compact connected minimal surface bounded by a pair of convex planar curves topologically an annulus?
accepted.context_brief: Topology of minimal surfaces with convex planar boundary

evidence.quote: Problem 6.1 (Meeks [125, 129, 126], 1978). Is every compact connected minimal surface bounded by a pair of convex planar curves topologically an annulus?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an embedded compact surface of constant mean curvature that is bounded by a circle but is not a piece of a sphere?
accepted.context_brief: Embedded CMC surface bounded by a circle

evidence.quote: Problem 6.2 (Earp, Fabiano, Meeks, and Rosenberg [50], 1991). Does there exist an embedded compact surface of constant mean curvature which is bounded by a circle, but is not a piece of a sphere.

accepted.question_text: Show that any compact embedded constant-mean-curvature surface that is bounded by a convex planar curve and lies entirely on one side of the plane containing that boundary curve must be topologically a disk.
accepted.context_brief: Half-space topology of embedded CMC surfaces

evidence.quote: Problem 6.3 (Ros and Rosenberg [156], 1996). Show that any compact embedded CMC surface which is bounded by a convex planar curve, and lies on one side of the boundary plane, is topologically a disk.

accepted.question_text: Are there any complete negatively curved surfaces in Euclidean 3-space whose principal curvatures are bounded away from zero?
accepted.context_brief: Negative curvature with principal curvatures bounded away from zero

evidence.quote: Problem 7.1 (Milnor [132], 1972). Are there any complete surfaces of negative curvature in Euclidean 3-space whose principal curvatures are bounded away from zero?

accepted.question_text: Are there any complete negatively curved surfaces embedded in the unit ball?
accepted.context_brief: Hadamard problem for unit ball embeddings

evidence.quote: Problem 7.2 (Hadamard [90, 27, 159], 1898). Are there any complete negatively curved surfaces embedded in the unit ball?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a complete negatively curved surface with negative Euler characteristic that is contained between a pair of parallel planes in Euclidean 3-space R3?
accepted.context_brief: Negatively curved surfaces between parallel planes

evidence.quote: Problem 7.3. Does there exist any complete negatively curved surfaces with negative Euler characteristic contained in between a pair of parallel planes in R3.

accepted.question_text: Show that every closed convex surface in Euclidean 3-space R3 has at least two umbilic points.

evidence.quote: Problem 8.1 (Carathéodory, 1922). Show that every closed convex surface in R3 has at least two umbilic points.

accepted.question_text: Show that any isolated singularity of a principal line field on a surface has index at most one.

evidence.quote: All the works mentioned thus far have been primarily concerned with establishing the analytic version of a local conjecture attributed to Loewner, which states that Problem 8.2 (Loewner). Show that the index of any singularity of a principal line fields on a surface is at most one.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a complete noncompact convex surface in R3 with principal curvatures k1 and k2. Must inf_M |k1 - k2| equal 0, meaning that the surface has umbilic behavior arbitrarily far out?

evidence.quote: Problem 8.3 (Toponogov [183], 1995). Let M be a complete noncompact convex surface in R3, with principal curvatures k1, k2, then show that infM |k1 − k2| = 0.
In other words, Toponogov suggests that every complete noncompact convex surface must have an umbilic "at infinity".
